title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Problem 1 of E297 and states Problem 2. Problem 1 asks for the first variation of a higher-order functional J[y] = ∫_0^a Z(x,y,p,q,r,s,…) dx, with p=y', q=y'', r=y''', s=y''''. The partial derivatives are written N=Z_y, P=Z_p, Q=Z_q, R=Z_r, S=Z_s.

The previous page did repeated integration by parts and obtained
δJ = ∫ δy (N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − …) dx
 + δy (P − Q' + R'' − S''' + …)
 + δy' (Q − R' + S'' − …)
 + δy'' (R − S' + …)
 + δy''' (S − …).
The boundary terms are evaluated at the endpoint. The top of this page adds that δy is the increment of the final value of y, while dδy, ddδy, … depend also on the increments of neighbouring values. So δy, δy', δy'', … at the endpoint are independent.

Coroll. 1. For J to be extremal the variation must vanish for arbitrary δy. Hence the higher-order Euler–Poisson (Euler–Lagrange) equation N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − … = 0 must hold at every interior point.

Coroll. 2. This is an ODE of order 2n. Its integration brings in arbitrary constants, so extra conditions can be imposed, such as prescribed values of y at given x (fixed boundary values).

Coroll. 3. If no such conditions are imposed, one may ask how to choose the constants so as to get the 'maximum maximorum' or 'minimum minimorum'. This yields the natural (free-endpoint, transversality) boundary conditions at x=a:
 P − Q' + R'' − S''' = 0, Q − R' + S'' = 0, R − S' = 0, S = 0.

Coroll. 4. By Euler's convention the variation is taken to vanish at x=0. The constant of integration in the integral part then forces the same boundary expressions to vanish at x=0 as well. So the natural boundary conditions hold at both ends.

Problem 2 is stated: Z depends also on a nonlocal quantity Φ(x) = ∫_0^x 𝔷(x,y,p,q,…) dx, with dZ = L dΦ + M dx + N dy + … and d𝔷 = 𝔐 dx + 𝔑 dy + …. The task is to find δ∫_0^a Z dx. The next page solves it with V = ∫ L dx normalised to vanish at x=a. This amounts to an adjoint or multiplier variable, giving the modified Euler equation with N − V𝔑, P − V𝔓, etc.
errors: Coroll. 4 argues awkwardly. Euler's convention that 'the variation must vanish at x=0' is imposed through an integration constant. The cleaner statement is that δJ = [boundary terms] evaluated from 0 to a, and that for free endpoints each bracket must vanish at both ends. Euler's conclusion is correct for free endpoints.

Coroll. 3 treats free-endpoint optimisation as optimising over the integration constants ('maximum maximorum'). This is valid heuristically but not rigorous. It also tacitly assumes the endpoint values δy, δy', δy'', … are all independent, which Euler justifies only informally in the first lines of the page.

ideas.what: Euler–Poisson equation for Lagrangians with derivatives up to order n, derived by integration by parts (δ-method)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744, by geometric method); Lagrange (1760–61, δ-method); Poisson for the name
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744); E296 Elementa calculi variationum; this paper E297

ideas.what: Natural boundary conditions for higher-order functionals at both endpoints (P − Q' + R'' − … = 0, …, S = 0)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (Essai, Misc. Taurinensia 1760–61) for boundary terms; Euler in E296/E297
ideas.where_published: E297 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 10, 1766); also Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E387)

ideas.what: Free-endpoint problem viewed as choosing integration constants to obtain the 'maximum maximorum'
ideas.modern_name: optimisation over the family of extremals / free-boundary variational problem

ideas.what: Functional whose integrand depends on a running integral Φ = ∫𝔷 dx (nonlocal / isoperimetric-type dependence)
ideas.modern_name: nonlocal Lagrangian; leads to adjoint (costate) variable V, akin to Lagrange multiplier / Pontryagin costate

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard first-variation material: the higher-order Euler–Poisson equation, natural boundary conditions, and the setup for integrands with nonlocal Φ. It is all well documented in Euler's E65, E296/E297 and the later Institutiones, and in Lagrange's work. Nothing appears to be absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially faithful to the image. In Coroll. 4 the image reads 'iisdem hisce aequationibus satisfiat', which matches the transcription.
In Coroll. 3 the first equation in the image ends with '− d³S/dx³ = 0' (no 'etc.'), as transcribed.
